artifacts.synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

artifacts.synopsis: Northern California Presbytery adopted an abstract resolution declaring six different views on the diaconate permissible for ministers and Sessions; the SJC sustained the complaints and annulled the resolution, holding that no court may issue binding abstract decrees beyond its proper jurisdictional exercise. A concurring opinion analyzed each of the six diaconal views in detail and set out standards (the GUMP/Kniseley framework) for when diaconal assistant practices are constitutionally permissible.

artifacts.title: Phelps v. Pacific Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Phelps complained that Pacific Presbytery erred by finding no constitutional irregularities in the New Life Burbank Session's ordination of Lee Irons as a ruling elder, despite PP's earlier refusal to receive Irons as a teaching-elder candidate. The SJC denied the complaint. Under BCO 39-3.3, the Court owed great deference to the lower court's discretionary fitness judgment; the single office of elder does not require identical eligibility processes, and the NLB Session had jurisdiction after Irons renounced OPC jurisdiction. PP's action stood; the SJC declined to decide the NAPARC issue.

artifacts.synopsis: The complaint challenged Presbytery’s commissions and its response to a canceled congregational meeting. The SJC upheld the Inman Commission because a Session may reference limited duties without congregational consent. It sustained the challenges to Presbytery’s consideration of the August 7 meeting and appointment of the Sealy Commission because the Session majority had validly canceled the meeting. Linton’s and Pellom’s calls therefore remained undissolved and Neville was uncalled, absent later congregational action. The SJC also upheld Presbytery’s criticism of the cancellation as unwise and its refusal to issue a BCO 40-5 citation.

artifacts.synopsis: A complaint challenged Presbytery’s suspension of a church Session and installation of a commission to perform Session functions without prior congregational consent. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled all subsequent commission actions as the Session insofar as the commission was improperly constituted. Presbytery could not suspend elected officers and replace them without prior consent; later recognition could not cure the defect. The SJC also rejected Presbytery’s objection that a related appeal barred the complaint because the cases presented fundamentally different issues.

artifacts.synopsis: Complainants challenged a Session plan under which most elders voluntarily resigned, the Session granted severance and benefits to its former pastor, proposed about a year with an interim pastor before a permanent call, and contemplated revising local bylaws. The SJC denied all four items. It held that the BCO permitted jointly considered voluntary resignations, that severance concerned resignation and the budget rather than a pastoral call, and that the plan and bylaw proposal were not themselves unconstitutional. Any later call still had to follow the BCO without undue delay, and local bylaws had to remain consistent with it.

artifacts.synopsis: A congregation member complained that New River Presbytery erred in November 1991 by declining to accept TE Don Post Jr.'s resignation and dissolve his pastoral relation, instead appointing a commission. The SJC sustained the complaint. Under BCO 23-1, once the congregation concurred and no sufficient reasons to retain the pastor appeared, the resignation 'shall be accepted' and the relation dissolved; the Presbytery's general BCO 13-9 power did not override that specific provision. The Presbytery had already dissolved the relation on December 7, 1991; the adopted judgment ordered no remand. Three commissioners dissented.

artifacts.synopsis: After a congregation voted to ask that all ruling elders' official relationships be dissolved without censure, the Session concurred and requested an interim Session. The SJC denied the elders' complaint, holding that BCO 24-6b extends by good and necessary deduction from one elder to multiple identified elders. Dissolution ended their service on that Session but did not divest them of office. Because both the congregation and Session requested it, BCO 13-9 and 15-2 authorized Presbytery to appoint an interim Session. A separate constitutional inquiry was denied without explanation.

artifacts.title: Nickoley and Stephens v. Southwest Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Complainants challenged Southwest Presbytery's January 1991 actions: withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving Pastor Pollock's pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of Covenant PC's session. The SJC did not sustain the complaint and affirmed. It held the BCO gives no presbytery authority to suspend a session or act as a Session pro tem without formal congregational consent; BCO 31-1 left the elder charges with the session, so they were never validly before Presbytery; the dissolution challenge was moot after Pollock left the PCA, though Presbytery acted correctly on the congregation's request.

artifacts.synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. But it affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals admitting no officer exception. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

artifacts.title: Melton et al. v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Complainants challenged the ruling of the session of Westminster Presbyterian Church (Chattanooga) disallowing proxy votes at a December 10, 1989 congregational meeting that voted not to rescind the earlier dissolution and property transfer to New City Fellowship. The SJC denied all specifications, holding that proxy voting was not required under BCO 24-4 or Robert's Rules, and that the congregation's decision to dissolve was within its rights under BCO Chapter 25.

artifacts.synopsis: A complaint challenged Philadelphia Presbytery’s approval of proceedings that cleared teaching and ruling elders without properly trying serious public accusations arising from Christ Church’s division. All three specifications were sustained because plea bargaining, dropped charges, and failure to hear necessary witnesses left the accusations unresolved. Presbytery’s action was annulled and de novo trials produced mixed convictions and acquittals. Harold Burkhart received six months’ suspension, Douglas McCready an admonition, and six former ruling elders three-month suspensions. The decision stressed taking such conflicts to Presbytery or judicial process rather than the congregation.

artifacts.title: Whether congregation may dissolve the session by vote
